fixes.explanation: Paul is the apostle writing this letter, and he doesn't point at himself. He points higher: “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children…” (Ephesians 5:1). Plenty of writers would slip their own name in as the pattern. Paul tells the believers to imitate God.

That's the answer: False. Paul writes, “For of this you can be sure: No immoral, impure, or greedy person (that is, an idolater) has any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” (Ephesians 5:5). He opens with “…you can be sure…” so there's nothing here to haggle over. I've tried haggling with my oven timer, and it never works either.

A coward isn't in this verse. The note in the parentheses reads “…(that is, an idolater)…”. Paul tucks it in right after “greedy person,” and it's easy to bite right past, like a chocolate chip hiding in thick dough.

Paul doesn't call anyone a liar here. His note sits right after the words “greedy person” and says “…(that is, an idolater)…”. It's one short phrase, and I've missed smaller things than that in my own bakery, like a timer I set and never heard.

That's it. Paul says, “Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience.” (Ephesians 5:6). He warns against being deceived with empty words, and then he names what is coming. It's the wrath of God.

Yes, he does. Paul writes, “…everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.” (Ephesians 5:13). The light doesn't just show things, it says what it shines on becomes light too. True is the answer, baker.

The verse says it does. Paul writes, “But everything exposed by the light becomes visible, for everything that is illuminated becomes a light itself.” (Ephesians 5:13). So the light makes things visible, and what it shines on becomes light itself. That makes True the answer.

That's the promise. The saying goes, “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you.” (Ephesians 5:14). It tells the sleeper to wake up and rise, and it says Christ will shine on him. Paul introduces it with “So it is said…” so he's passing along a saying.

The world's will isn't in this verse. Paul says, “Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.” (Ephesians 5:17). It's the Lord's will that he wants them to understand. He sets that against being foolish.

Yes, the Spirit. Paul says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18). He warns against getting drunk on wine, and the one to be filled with is the Spirit. Notice he doesn't just say stop. He says what to take up instead.
